question: The under-representation of Central and Eastern European countries, including Poland, among the staff of the European External Action Service is structural and is particularly evident in management positions and among EU Heads of Delegation. I already drew attention to this issue back in 20241.

In response to my question, the VicePresident of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy gave an assurance that she was working towards a more balanced representation of the Member States that have joined the EU since 2004, and was monitoring the geographical balance in the EEAS2.

However, the latest appointments made by the VicePresident / High Representative as part of the EEAS rotation exercise suggest the opposite. Among the 33 nominated EU Ambassadors and the seven Deputy Heads of Delegation, there are no Polish nationals, despite 13 candidates having applied.
Moreover, of the 40 new appointments, only a small proportion were given to nationals of the countries that have joined the EU since 2004. In this connection: 1.

Why is there no one from Poland among the latest appointments, especially considering the country’s size, its location on the eastern border of the EU and its particular role in EU security, as well as the fact that 13 Polish candidates applied?
Since providing an answer to Question E-003067/2024, what action has the EEAS taken to improve the geographical balance of the representatives of the countries that have joined the EU since 2004?

Since December 2024, how many special events and information sessions on opportunities for employment and career progression at the EEAS have been either held in Poland or targeted at potential candidates from Poland?

Joint answer given by High Representative/Vice-President Kallas on behalf of the European Commission (28 October 2026) European External Action Service (EEAS) recruitment and selection procedures are based on merit, while ensuring adequate geographical and gender balance.
Since 2024, all Central and Eastern European countries have had at least one national appointed in a middle management position and since 2025 all of them have at least one Head of Delegation post.

In Poland’s case, there are currently five Ambassadors serving in EU Delegations and three senior managers serving at headquarters: the Director for Security and Defence Policy; the Director for Security and Corporate Services and the Managing Director for Europe and Central Asia who will be joining the EEAS as in November 2026.

In its contacts with Member States, the EEAS encourages them to put forward a sufficient number of well-prepared candidates and provides guidance on the qualifications expected. Information sessions are organised for candidates participating in the rotation. In the case of Poland, a dedicated session was organised ahead of rotation 2026.

Discussions also took place in the framework of the EEAS Human Resources Network; one of its meetings in which Polish representatives took part was specifically dedicated to preparing national candidates. The EEAS remains committed to continued engagement with all Member States, in order to support strong candidacies and to improve geographical balance over time.
